data.title: JavaScript Is Single-Threaded
data.subtitle: One call stack per realm; async delegates to the host

cards.meaning: Per realm (tab main world, Worker, Node isolate): one JS call stack; at most one JS turn runs at a time. Sync code runs to completion before queued callbacks for that realm start.

cards.front: Does single-threaded JS mean the browser/Node has one OS thread?
cards.meaning: No. Host work (network, disk, crypto) can use other OS threads. The claim is one JS call stack per realm, not one OS thread for the whole process. Interview phrasing: user JS on the main thread is single-threaded; concurrency of waiting is host-side; parallel JS computation needs Workers or extra processes.

cards.front: What is the JS call stack?
cards.meaning: The LIFO structure of function frames currently executing. While c runs inside b inside a, the stack is roughly a → b → c. When c returns, frames pop until the stack is empty for that turn of work.
cards.example: function a() { b(); } function b() { c(); } function c() { console.log('c'); } a();

cards.front: When can a queued callback start — does await pause the JS thread?
cards.meaning: Only when the engine starts a new turn, which requires the previous turn's stack to be empty. Nothing interleaves into the middle of a running function unless that function yields (e.g. await). await schedules a continuation for later; it does not pause the thread like an OS blocking wait.

cards.front: Does async mean another JS thread?
cards.meaning: No. Async hands waiting work (timers, I/O, network) to the host (Web APIs, libuv), returns immediately, and runs callbacks later on the same JS thread when the stack is empty and the event loop picks them. A pending fetch is the network stack waiting, not another JS thread sitting in your function.

cards.front: What happens when you call setTimeout / fetch / fs.readFile?
cards.meaning: Not another JS thread that sits and waits. (1) JS calls a host API. (2) The host registers work. (3) The JS call returns immediately; the stack continues. (4) Later the host queues a callback/task/microtask. (5) The event loop runs that callback on the same single JS thread when allowed.

cards.front: log start; setTimeout(0); log end — order?
cards.meaning: start, end, then timeout. setTimeout only schedules; sync code in the same turn finishes first; the callback runs in a later turn after the stack clears (and after microtasks for that phase).
cards.example: console.log('start'); setTimeout(() => console.log('timeout'), 0); console.log('end'); // start, end, timeout

cards.front: Non-blocking I/O vs concurrent requests vs parallel JS?
cards.meaning: Non-blocking I/O: the JS thread is not stuck waiting on slow I/O; the host waits and enqueues a callback — many operations can be in flight, JS callbacks still serialized. Parallel JS on the main thread is false — still one stack. Parallel JS with Workers: separate stacks; communicate via messages.

cards.front: Where does concurrency live if not on the JS stack?
cards.meaning: Browser Web APIs (timers, fetch, DOM events) plus other rendering machinery; Node libuv/OS (network, timers, filesystem via the thread pool, DNS). Many waits run elsewhere; your callback still runs single-threaded when it fires. A blocked main thread still starves input handlers and often janks paint; Node callbacks still serialize unless you use worker_threads.

cards.front: Why does a 3s busy while loop delay setTimeout(0)?
cards.meaning: The timer may fire in host time, but the JS callback cannot start until the stack empties. Order: start, end, then (after ~3s of blocking) timer. While the loop occupies the stack, no other JS on that realm runs — UI/React handlers and Nest request handlers on that process wait. Don't blame the event loop; queues cannot preempt running JS.
cards.example: console.log('start'); setTimeout(() => console.log('timer'), 0); while (Date.now() < end) {} console.log('end');

cards.meaning: Delay is a minimum, not a guarantee — “when the timer is eligible and the loop gets to that task,” not the next CPU instruction. The callback goes to the timer/macrotask queue; it never runs synchronously, even at 0ms. Code after the setTimeout call still runs first. Browsers may clamp nested timers; still never inline sync.

sync, then microtask, then timeout. Microtasks (Promise .then, queueMicrotask) scheduled in the same turn run before the next timer macrotask. setTimeout(0) is not “before all Promise callbacks.” Full rules belong in the event-loop unit.
cards.example: setTimeout(() => console.log('timeout'), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('microtask')); console.log('sync'); // sync, microtask, timeout

cards.front: Workers and the single-thread story — is JS therefore multi-threaded?
cards.meaning: Each Worker is a separate realm with its own single JS thread and stack; message-passing (structured clone / transferables), not a shared call stack or lexical this. Main-thread JS stays single-threaded. Do not say JS is multi-threaded because Workers exist — parallelism is another realm, still single-threaded inside itself.
cards.notes: Browser: Worker, SharedWorker. Node: worker_threads or cluster/processes.

cards.front: Do async functions / await run on another thread?
cards.meaning: No — same thread until await; await schedules the continuation later on that thread. await does not invent threads or OS-block inside the engine the way a sync loop does.

cards.front: Does creating a Promise parallelize CPU?
cards.meaning: No — work before the first await is sync and blocking; a Promise only models async completion and queues reactions. Single-threaded still allows concurrency of waiting; it does not mean parallel JS on the same stack.

cards.front: Practical consequences of long sync CPU?
cards.meaning: Prefer async I/O over readFileSync on servers. Break huge CPU: chunking, scheduling, Workers, or native addons. In React/RN, expensive sync work in render/effects blocks interactions. In NestJS, CPU-heavy work in a request handler blocks the event loop for other requests on that process.

cards.front: Closures vs single-threading — which vs when?
cards.meaning: Closures still decide which variables a callback sees when it eventually runs. Single-threading decides when that callback is allowed to run relative to other JS.
